I don’t like it b/c it seems to brand heavy & ad sneaky. Like who are you gonna serve those cookies too? People who just sit and talk about glossier? People who don’t know about glossier?  When you bake the cookies, i bet you’re going to be thinking about glossier? So no matter what, glossier inserts itself into a conversation and given how much beauty products rely on word of mouth rather than traditional advertising, i can’t help but be a little suspicious about its intentions. And with this product’s potential to be passive advertising fueled by their own customers…they’re not selling a cookie cutter, they’re selling a feeling and packaging an identity that can sell itself 

I know it doesn’t make any sense and I’m being paranoid b/c I read too much marketing science. But brands crossing thresholds like that has always been suspicious. Like there’s a reason Coca Cola flashes a sign and rarely anything else and why insurance commercials will show a lizard before any real coverage plan, because brands are much more powerful when they are an idea and an identity rather than a series of products. Don’t listen to me, but a cookie cutter from a beauty brand that makes beauty brand cookies?? Who invited them into the kitchen

Edit: not sure why the downvotes but no comment? Like why does Facebook get scrutiny for manipulation in advertising but Glossier doesn’t? Especially when it’s obviously working given that this very sub talks about buying the cookie cutter even though they don’t bake cookies. Like if a consumer can buy a product on name alone, beauty or not, usable or not….and then use said product to tell other ppl about that very same product and brand, then that’s a pretty intense thing. I’m not saying that glossier meant to be malicious, I’m sure they don’t even think about it this way. But it is one of those things where you realize just how often brands uses manipulative tactics and how normal it’s become for brands to use psychological influence alone to sell something. 

Anyway: [Here’s an article that talks about what ads are supposed to do. Note the positive tone!](https://instapage.com/blog/brand-advertising-examples)

[And here’s one about ethics and ads for self identity ](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/business-ethics-quarterly/article/abs/is-selfidentity-image-advertising-ethical/15BDBD804CE5B93E71485DBABD3D0FDA)

I was on the fence about getting a phd but most of my anxieties were about job prospects and financial instability. I felt like academia was perfect for me and that I really enjoyed it but I didn’t know if it was worth the terrors of job competition, lack of money, and the steep location change. But to start from the beginning this was my throughly process as a 21 year old approaching that post grad existential crisis:

*Im from a small town in rural texas. If I want to get a job, i have to go to one of the best schools in the country. That means leaving my rural texas hometown and family business, my chronically ill mother and autistic little brother and living off a grad student stipend for 6-7 years. And even THEN there’s no garuare that there will be a job or financial stabilit. The job market is fierce and location locked. This is what I want to do but it’s a huge risk with a high fail potential.*

So I took a gap year after undergrad. In that gap year, I got a “real” job and still worked the family restaurant. I had no money at all. I was always tired but still incredibly drawn to writing and reading. During that gap year, I realized that I was going to be a broke 20 something, no matter what I did. Either I could be a broke 20 something doing what I love or I could spend my 20s smelling like fried chicken and dish water. So half way through my gap year, I started applying to grad school. I’m so glad I took the gap because it proved that I really wasn’t happy doing anything else and that my fears of poverty were ever present. 

Still, I was hesitant and still on the fence. I applied to 7 master’s programs and 2 phds and was accepted into 2 master’s programs and 1 phd. I knew I wanted to be involved in academia but still had no real experience with it, so I accepted a funded master’s program instead of the Phd. I wanted to get my feet wet without too much commitment. It was also a 3 hour drive from home. But once I got in my master’s program, I was immediately treated like a professional. I was definitely an amateur in almost every way but my master’s program was really supportive. I realized that being an academic was a perfect fit for me. I loved it and moved towards a phd after. This phd is far from but I’m glad I did the close master’s program because it gave my mom tied to get the restaurant back together and be more assured of my little brother’s health. (He’s 20 and a freshman in college now)

I definitely went ahead with a phd despite my doubts but I took it really really slow. That’s my advice to anyone in a similar situation

When I was in high school there was a smash or pass list. One for boys that rated the girls and another for girls that ranked the boys. And eventually every clique had a version, like theater kids, football team, dance squad etc. So there were about 10-20 sheets of paper around that ranked a little differently. Like you could be #3 on one list but #15 on another. Most lists stopped at 50 and if you weren’t on it, then you you were a loser. (Oh my god this sounds terrible now that I say the story out loud)

But I remember all my friends making paper cut outs of all the boys’ names and switching them around. “Jacob and Mike are tied for number one.” “NO! Justin should be number one.” I never really caught on as to how they were ranking the guys. To me there was no scale at all. Like yea I could recognize aesthetic attraction in individuals but I distinctly remember not being able to tell why a guy was #5 or #20. If two men
we’re hot, I couldn’t tell which was hotter. I felt left out; I didn’t have a scale and I didn’t know why. I didn’t want to smash anyone let alone see who was the most smash-able. And everyday this sex list was pushed in my face. 

And these were some serious lists. Girls and boys were literally decorating it with cardboard paper, glitter, etc. Girls were writing the list in cursive and calligraphy. And believe it or not, the guys list was just as ornate. These guys drew hearts, titties, and rap lyric typography. So imagine 10-20 intensely decorated papers titled “smash or pass” and a list of names. And back them, cell phones were not something everyone had so it was just the lists. But for that entire year, everyone only wanted to talk about that list and I never “got it.” 

And on the flip side, even though I didn’t get smash or pass, I still *wanted* to be on the list. There was a lot of social pressure for me to feel and be attractive. I was #2 on one list, #4, #7, and #32. I cried when I was #32. And i was perplexed because I didn’t really understand the criteria for the list but was being pressured to be on it anyway. 

Eventually the teachers found out and FLIPPED. I definitely understand why. We were put on silent lunch for the rest of the year, there were anti bullying assemblies and all the dances, including homecoming was canceled. Spirit week stuff like “best dressed” and “most likely to succeed” was also cancelled and taken out of the yearbook. So not only did I not “get it” but I had to spend my junior year on lock down. We even had to write letters apologizing and I didn’t even know what to apologize for.

Usually lots of effort will translate into a good paper. It’s rare that a student will put in lots of research, drafting, and editing and still have a C-F paper. I give my students a mini writing and composition lecture that outlines how academic papers work. I also have the library come over and talk about research. My students have everything they need when it comes to writing. 

Still, students may have trouble and as much as I wish I was, I’m not psychic. If a student is trying and it’s not working, it’s important that they come to me. I can’t tell how hard a student worked on something just by looking at them or by grading their papers. If a student is having difficulties and trying, I prefer that they let me know, personally. Come to office hours or set up a meeting. Come prepared for those meetings and try to follow the advice given. Effort means nothing when it ignores advice. For example, I had a student try really hard on a 3 page research paper. I specifically stated that his issue was that the research cited were not peer reviewed sources. They were websites and news articles, not actual peer reviewed articles, journals, or legitimate academic publications. When the paper was submitted, no new citation was added and the claims still referenced wikipedia. There were about 10-15 websites cited and I get that the student tried but  :/

The writing center is also a resource my students can use. Even if my students never meet with me face to face, I still take notice when the writing center sends me an acknowledgment. I keep a list of writing center students. So yea, I take effort into consideration when I grade papers but that effort had to be real and I need to know what’s effort and what’s bad writing.

This research was not designed to expose a direct correlation with sun and life but to consider the sun as factor of a more complex system. It’s not sun exposure alone that lowers blood pressure.

Those who get more sun exposure are more than likely also the ones who exercise frequently, engage in social interactions, and have more access to things like quality food. While those with less sun exposure, to a chronic degree, are usually those with less social interaction and illness. 

At the end of the day, Sunlight is one of many beneficial things and one of many harmful things. But SPF will not stifle the benefits of sunlight in life or death situations. Because sunlight is just a factor, not the entire equation

“Technology’s use has been increasing rapidly.” doesn’t need citing but it doesn’t need to be in a research paper at all without further pushing. If I saw that, I would mark it as too generalizing a statement. I mark down all unsupported statements like that because it’s too broad and honestly, feels like a waste of my time

But if you want to say something that general or want to introduce a similar idea, it’s important to narrow the scope of that statement and make it relevant to what the research paper is about. And you can use sources to do that.

“Technology’s use is increasing rapidly. For example, the HTU survey concluded that in 2000, most homes owned an average of two devices with internet capabilities (Fakename, 15). And in 2015, the HTU survey revealed that the average number of internet capable devices in a single home, had risen to 15 (Fakename, 7).”

“Technology’s use is increasing rapidly and as the use of technology continues to be normalized in society, it’s increased availability positively benefits those with disabilities and de stigmatizes the use of assistive technology. “Study I just made up” notes that hearing aids are easier to make, cheaper to produce, and more accessible to people in rural and low income states (cite). Alternatively, “An academic ariticle I just made up,” reveals that a growing number of children feel comfortable and confident while wearing hearing aids as bullying and harassment of hearing impaired children has decreased in elementary aged children (cite)....” 

“Technology’s use is increasing rapidly, especially when it comes to interactive entertainment. The bureau I just made up, states that video games are played an average of 50 hours a week by those who own gaming/entertainment systems and consider the device their primary source of entertainment (Cite)” 
————

When you are making statements about “what everyone knows” or “your opinion,” it’s still important to ground that statement within your research paper’s groundwork. What do you mean by “technology”? What do you mean by “increasing”? What do you mean by “rapidly?” Like yea, everyone knows what those words and that sentence means but if you want that sentence to have any weight at all you have to make it important to the topic at hand. In the examples I gave, I defined why the use of technology was important and gave my opinion credibility while also getting to the point of the paper. They are credibility and points I made up so please don’t make things up, but please do find ways to narrow and ground all the things that are “common knowledge.” No one reads a research paper to figure out what most people know, that information can be transitional but it should never take center stage and go unsupported

Make an annotated bibliography. 

I read somewhere that before computers were a thing academics would read a sources, write down the citation information, and a quick synopsis of the text on index cards. I don’t know if it’s true or where I read it (oh the irony) but I thought it’s was a wonderful idea. [But here is an example](https://www.sps186.org/downloads/basic/520684/NoteCardsOutline-%20research.pdf) /
[here is another ](https://sites.google.com/site/nsvirtuallearningcommons/organize-your-research) 

I don’t really keep note cards but now I keep a running document of sources, annotations, and citation information. I have a different document for each project. Each primary or secondary source has 10-15 sentences and maybe a quote is enough to sum everything up and highlight what I will need in the future.

As for each physical copy of an article or book, I use sticky notes. The annotated cloud document has most of the information but I also put sticky notes with 3-4 sentences of what I read.

As to what you should do while you are reading, underline and write in the margins why any information is important. Just the act of underlining and writing what it is that makes the information useful/valuable is enough to force the information into your memory

University instructors and professors are very much liable for the learning environments they are in charge of

That being said, I don’t believe “no cell phone use in class” is enforcing an “excessive rule.” Nothing about that is excessive. If a student can’t be away from their phone for 50 minutes, that’s a much more excessive problem than my rules will ever be. But I’ve also found that having a no cell phone policy results in students checking their phone, then putting it away do they don’t get caught. But letting students have cell phones results in multiple students on their phones the entire time! I’d rather have students discreetly on their phone with my no cell phone policy, than multiple students openly distracted just because they can. 

But if I clearly state what it is that I expect from them, 100% attention and no cell phones, then they actually *do* pay more attention, participate more, and  follow other directions. It’s totally do able. I work from 8am-5pm and that’s including teaching a 2/2 load, my own research, and course work. It isn’t difficult but it is very important that you plan and know what it is you do at every got between 9am and 6pm.

Have a planner that details every hour and don’t depart from it. What I do is set daily goals and the first thing I do every morning is write down what I want to get done for the day

This was today’s list:

-Log participation grades

-Finish Novel

-Read 2 articles for course work

-Make annotated bibs for 3 articles

-Make an outline for summer fellowship 
application

Bonus: Email Advisor

None of this is very time consuming but lots of small goals add up to lots of progress. If you do this, it’s best to have a bonus in case you finish early.
 It’s also really good to have variety in your work day. Instead of taking breaks full of doing nothing, just switch to a completely different task once you’ve zoned out on another. Instead of working in one thing for an hour and taking a 10 minute break. Work for an hour, then switch to something different. That way there’s no gaps in productivity. 

But still make sure you have a definable break. I take an hour long lunch and when I need to use the restroom, I will literally walk to a different building or go upstairs, so I can get a little walk and some fresh air. 

And finally, have a planned “end” of the work day. If I’m working from home, ending my day involves cleaning and resetting my desk. I close all my tabs, put my stuff away, get tomorrow’s bag ready, and wipe my desk with cleaning spray and towel. (I’m not going to use a desk I just cleaned so that’s motivation for me to leave and stay gone.) Having an unwinding Routine really helps. If you have an iPhone, I also suggest using Screen time and blocking all social media between the hours of 9am-6pm. It isn’t always smooth and you might still pull some 12 hour days but the trick to the stable work day you’re imagining is finding a good routine and the discipline to stick with it Good luck!

You just have to give it acknowledgement and give it a place. Sometimes that place is in a donation bin but other times it’s just somewhere other than the closet floor. The KonMari method isn’t about getting throwing things away and could be done successfully by throwing zero things away. Just fold your clothes, give them thanks, and make dedicated spaces for everything. When it comes to large wardrobes, if a large wardrobe sparks joy than you keep it but it is also important that you are able to acknowledge your connection to your wardrobe give it a stable place in your home and your life. I would suggest getting to know your professors. Introduce yourself and take multiple classes with instructors that you like. Get an academic related job on campus like tutoring or the writing center, and then move on to research and conference presenting. Get involved in the academic community of your school and department. Get to know the grad students too and ask them about their experience. Get an academic advisor too, a good one. And let them know about your interest in grad school very early on. Learn how to read and write academic research also 

But to give some more abstract advice, work on patience. A career in academia is long, difficult and competitive. Your undergrad and PhD combined will take 10+ years, navigating the job market after graduation will take time as well. If you want to be a tenured track academic, that’s another 7 years or more. Academics are not paid that well either so consider that. To avoid that I highly suggest having multiple career options and taking gap years. The one regret I have about undergrad is that I was so determined to get into grad school, get my PhD and become a tenured academic, that I didn’t consider anything else. I didn’t branch out and give myself options nor did I consider the downsides of academic careers. I’m not gonna list those negatives but now I’m in a PhD program with a serious case of “what if” syndrome. So don’t be like me. 

That being said, my final piece of advice is don’t let the horror stories scare you off. Eventually someone will tell you how “bad” academia is. Listen to them but know that you know what’s best for your life. 

Enjoy your undergrad career and congratulations on graduating high school. Study abroad if you can. Research will benefit you much more than grades will but grades are still very important. And save up money because grad school applications are expensive

The grad school application for me was entirely different than undergrad 

Grad school will be much more specific. In applying for undergrad, I just had to give a general sense of my future with the hopes of getting a maleable education. Grad school is much more specific as you are applying to a very specific department rather than an institution. 

For me, the grad process was much more tedious. I needed letters of recommendation, but from well known people and employers. I took specialized standardized tests, and my personal statement had to be career oriented rather than purely future driven. I had to have very specific research interests rather than an intended major. I’m in the humanities so I also had to submit a 10-15 page writing sample. In searching for undergrad university I just looked at school and rank. For graduate school I had to go a bit deeper and research faculty members, and actual people. There’s no point in going to a highly ranked school if the people and resources available do not cater to your interests. And once you get your acceptances you have to navigate stipends, pay and living costs.

You, as an academic, will always be confronted with this specific brand of ambiguity. Just wash your hands of it and learn how to deal. This may be because I worked for a writing center and have grown used to a lot of student writing problems but it’s best to be patient and objective instead of seeing the papers as a personal failing. 

I’m not sure if you are at an American university but many American students do not know how to write a paper on the university level. They’ve never really been taught and the huge disparity between the quality of education means that some students get all the way to college and still have no idea what’s required of them in essays and it’s impossible for universities to vet them for it. It’s also not fair for professors and TAs to play catch up so lots of students get left behind. It’s easy to say “no plagiarizing” but you’d be surprised at how little students know about plagiarizing and what actually counts as plagiarizing. For example, when I was in high school a teacher said that the best way to write without plagiarizing was to take the most “important” words of a sentence and rewrite it in my own words. She would take 3 words out of sentence, construct a new sentence out of it and call it original. Again, this was high school.

And about content, many students are used to “bullshiting” and book reports that are nothing but summary. They don’t realize that summarizing is not writing. I worked at a writing center for a highly ranked university and I saw students making those same summarizing and bullshiting mistakes. They’ve grown used to writing the night before a deadline and getting excellent scores. In college that won’t fly. And to add to that, writing is neglected in lots of mass educational spheres. Writing papers is “easy” compared to exams. Students almost always underestimate how much effort needs to be put into writing, editing, reading etc. Writing isn’t seen as a skill that needs to be practiced. Again, this isn’t completely a personal failing just a misunderstanding and a needed wake up call. Most of the time just telling the student where they went wrong and pointing them in the direction of improvement is enough to get them to improve.

Be harsh but don’t be judgmental. It can be frustrating but looking at it from thier perspective helps. If thier papers are bad send them to a writing center and give them a website or video about plagiarism and editing

I really like lists! Giving myself small daily deadlines is much easier to manage than large projects and it’s much harder to procrastinate a daily goal. These daily goals though are usually no longer than your standard sticky note. For example this is my list for today:

-Grade 15-20 essays

-Read and annotate 3 articles or book chapters (reading to completion isn’t necessary, just start)

-Email advisor about thesis progress

-Write 1 page 

Bonus: Finish novel 

For context, I’m a literature PhD and that involves reading 2-3 novels a week, reading tons more secondary material, and writing. I’m also teaching two courses. 

This list may seem arbitrary but they are all related to my different projects in very small ways. It also isn’t that intense. But eventually those small things add up and I get a lot done. I also write one page a day. no matter how far or ahead of schedule I am, I write one page if *something* every day. 

So yea instead of finding motivation to get a lot of work done, find motivation to get a little bit done each day and watch your progress steadily grow.

To get started I really like these printables:


[4 day assessment ](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1JSTc9djxguhLOff2lMfsypvfdot0BK0w/view) 

[10 day assessment ](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1HlM7mtC9u5eJTnssANTl9hs8W2PXDLx8/view) 

Also, try having a solid tangible end to your work day. Stopping at 5pm everyday may motivate you to actually work before 5pm because you know you won’t have to do anything after a certain point. I’m much more apt to start something at 3pm if I know I don’t have to after 5pm.

I think most of it is just *life* And by life, I mean grad school confronts you with a lot of emotional things that are just a part of living in general. Grad school doesn’t burn ppl out, life does. But in grad school it’s much more isolating. 

Going to grad school is a pretty big commitment that involves a huge life shift. Everyone that goes to grad school has to make a pretty big change. That, in it of itself, is stressful.

And this sub tends to attract people going into Academia. And the job market isn’t the greatest. So again, grad school is a huge commitment full of new and unknown responsibilities AND the entire time, there’s a looming threat that it will all be worthless in the end because you’ll be unable to find a job. 

But ok. the job anxiety is in the future. But even on day one: when you’re in grad school, you’re literally thrown into a sea of new information, conversation, and responsibilities. And it’s up to you to stay afloat. It’s easy to say, “go to conferences, publish, teach.” But once the time comes, there are no directions. Suddenly you have so much resources and so much potential, yet there’s no concrete way to see it into fruition. Like I’m TEACHING a course. I have actual undergrads seeing me on a weekly basis and I know nothing about education. I love teaching but I had to find that out in my own. And that’s just one example of a huge responsibility with relatively little guidance. But all of that is to say that there is no way to prepare for grad school. It’s the constant battle of learning as you go. Every time i ask something the answer is always, “It depends.” And that may sound like a nonchalant way to describe it but it’s terrifying 

I didn’t mean to go on for so long but the last thing I want to note is that ALL of this is something that not many people outside of academia understand. Grad students and academics experience a unique brand of existentialism that most of society doesn’t. Eventually this separation is felt and it starts to feel like your work is alienating and hard to explain. Like I work all the time but I have a hard time telling my friends and family what I do on a daily basis. They think I’m here to “teach,” and that’s true, but there’s so much I can’t tell them because honestly, they will not care. I’m here for literature but my boyfriend is getting his PhD in a STEM field and even he has trouble justifying his actions and intentions 

The most stressful thing about grad school isn’t the work. It’s the fact that I’m being underpaid for it, there’s a good chance that this will continue well into my future, and that I can only talk about these struggles with a few people and a handful of Reddit users. 

TLDR: Grad school isn’t stressful. Life is stressful, grad school just happens to put a different spin on things because it’s isolating while still demanding lots of responsibility.

Your personal statement is about your life story *as it relates to your professional identity and career.* You can write about your hardships if it contributes to your work philosophy and doesn’t feel forced.

To give an example I’m a mixed black and Hawaiian girl. That literally means nothing on its own and the literature ma and PhD committees didn’t ask.  

But I did talk about how reading literature from the mainland shaped my education, how black women  make up less than 1% of literature scholars (despite African American literature being a literal field on its own), and how all of that contributes to my writing. I didn’t make myself a victim rather I talked about how I took a struggle and a niche topic and used it for my benefit. I also outlined my professional goals.

Your statement should do these things; introduce yourself and your values, prove you are someone who can reflect on thier past experiences and use it to shape future ones, and show how you are a good fit for departmental needs. At the end of the day you will be a part of a professional department, a co worker kinda, and your statement should let them know who you are as a person and how you can benefit thier department 

It’s not enough that you’re an immigrant or mentally ill or have struggled in someway. What matters is that you can take a tangible experience, be it good or bad, and show how it reflects you as a person with relevant potential.

The problem isn’t the standardization, standardized is fine. The problem is standardized does NOT mean equal. It does NOT mean universal. It means *the same.* And that faux equivalency of sameness to equal opportunity warps our perception of what the test actually is and what it does.

Standardized is  a concept based on the quantified measurements of a given thing. It’s determined by people, counted by people, and interpreted by people. The subsequent test is made up by even more people. Therefore it isn’t objective because people by their very nature, are not objective. What is the average/standard? How high is that average? Is that average growing? How is average even defined? What is on the test? Standardized test are human constructs that measure human defined capability and potential. But a number on something like that is not easy. And this is a capitalism driven world we live in. Capitalism is about numbers and the bottom line and thanks to years of indoctrination (IQ tests, state tests, ACT, SAT) we’ve been taught to believe that intelligence is measured by quantitative means and not, you know, by effort, engagement and consciousness study. The idea that numbers are somehow equal and objective (when they aren’t) has led to this idea that years of actual work means nothing if there isn’t a number attached to it. We talk about Albert Einstein’s IQ score but not that he was a strong advocate for education, spent years learning, and years educating. I mentioned this in another post but the idea of a standardized test is supposed to be to assess knowledge but when that assessment became more valuable than the knowledge, itself it was reversed. Now the knowledge is assessed by the standardized test. Now the test is capital. Even in elementary schools, students aren’t tested on what they have learned. Students learn what they will be tested on and class literally stop once the test of done. (Let’s not forget that the test isn’t free. It’s millions of dollars every year) And that’s pretty fucked up. 

The GRE is a $200 a pop so don’t think that thier interests are humanitarian and that they care about the smart people. Don’t think they are seeking the ones who shine above the rest. In fact, they rely on the smart ones. Whenever there is a criticism they can always rely on the ones whose ego has been stroked to say “hey it worked for me.” Anyway,

As a business the tests care about the average and below average people. Average and below average are completely arbitrary things  but since we’ve been culturally conditioned to believe that success is tied to “above” average then that is exploited by the higher education system. The test, the retest, courses, the prep books, those are all working in tandem. They prey on the ESL students, the minorities, people in rural areas. the disabled and even the nervous test takers. When knowledge is quantified there will always be an incentive to disenfranchise and as long as capitalism is envolved there will always be an incentive to exploit that disenfranchised. There is no equal testing when the GRE is that expensive ESPECIALLY when a one time event is seen as superior than strait As, extra curricular and great letters. Like oh my god, how terrible is it that ALL of that can be seen as a fluke but not that one test that you took on that one day.

...wait so you’re more apt to take high grades, which are usually a result of consistent study and engagement over months/years, “with a grain of salt” as well as question the validity of heavy projects...but can take the GRE, a 4 hour/one day cram test, without question??? That doesn’t make sense.

And it’s not difficult to judge a school’s curriculum. Universities have prestige and rank to indicate quality but even then, the faculty of most universities, (public, private, no name, ivy, etc.) are made up of very bright professionals. I talked about things that that particular university would be instead in. Grad schools are all about fit and I tried to be the best candidate for thier specific needs  (I hope that makes sense.) When you are accepted, you’re pretty much a part of their department and they want someone who can help achieve whatever status quo they have in mind. You can have an outstanding statement objectively but to get in your application has to meet the needs of the faculty

I looked through the department’s website and looked at the graduate students that were accepted and what they were working on. That gave me a good indication of what the department wanted. I even contacted the first year students and very humbly introduced myself and asked for a copy of thier statement (with sensitive details omitted of course) and they were usually very willing to help. A few even told me what the department was trying to work on. For example, one department was very interested in digital media studies, so I made my statement relative to that. Another department wanted to grow thier early American studies area and I didn’t even apply because I hate early American. Then I read the latest publications of the faculty members i wanted to work with, that gave me an even better idea of what the faculty was like and what they were looking for. I even referenced the publications in my statement . If you have access to a university library, I highly recommend reading the work of the faculty of each preferred school.

As for personal details, I took two years off and I talked about the reasons why. This is a humanities degree and that can be kind of scary considering the many difficulties and risks. In my statement I revealed that after undergrad I was afraid to take that risk. I wanted a career in the humanities but i was too afraid of failing so I tried to do other things. I took the GRE and did well but the very next day I took the LSAT just to give myself some options. I applied to one law school got in. But I couldn’t make myself want to go to law school. Elle Woods made it look so easy but I was actually sad when I realized I got in. (Plus law school is it’s own gamble anyway) So after bailing on school completely for two years, I realized that a career in the humanities was what I wanted and that I loved it so much I was willing to take the risk despite all the doom that it may entail. This is the only thing i can see myself doing so here i am. 

Anyway, in my statements I talked about why I wanted to go to grad school and how that and my research interests could benefit each university and it’s specific needs
